cells: MATHEMATICAL LIMITATION EXAMPLES  |  Stage-gated help, never a generic menu of weaknesses
First filter by the CURRENT STAGE in column K. C20–C26: collection/source/sampling/measurement ONLY. C40–C50: technique-specific mathematical limitations ONLY.
Then check route, confirmed real method/data and CURRENTLY USED mathematics (column L). A planned technique or prediction alone cannot trigger a calculation-specific example.
Show 2–3 optional matches at most, on request. 'Show more' stays within the SAME stage. Do not leak a later PMCC, regression or optimisation weakness into Data Collection.
At C60 Evaluation, revisit the limitations the STUDENT actually confirmed when doing earlier work and ask how these affect the conclusion; do not open a new unfiltered suggestions bank.
Every suggestion is a possibility, not a diagnosis. Allow None apply, student-written alternatives and return/review when a method changes. Never write the student's evaluation.

Statistics
Sampling: voluntary/convenience respondents (completion.data.sampleCensus or completion.stat.samplingImplementation)
Could volunteers differ systematically from the people you wanted to study?
Selection bias may change estimates, correlations or group differences; conclusions may not generalise beyond respondents.
Compare respondent composition with the target population or compare subgroups where possible.
A scoped analysis of these respondents may still answer a narrower question; avoid claims about all students.
Only suggest when selection was voluntary/opportunity or demonstrably nonrandom.
Review
Confirmed volunteer/opportunity selection and a stated target population; compare who responds with who is being represented.
Statistics
Sampling: simple random sample from an incomplete frame
AI13 / AA14
Might your sampling list exclude some members of the intended population?
Coverage bias remains possible even if selection FROM that list was genuinely random.
Compare the sampling frame with the target population and identify excluded groups.
State clearly what population the random selection actually represents.
Do not say random sampling itself causes bias; the possible issue is frame coverage.
Review
Actual random sample selected from a list that might exclude part of the target population.
Statistics
Sampling: stratified sample with unequal selection fractions
AI13 / AA14
Were some groups sampled at a different rate than their share of the target population?
Unweighted overall averages/percentages may overrepresent heavily sampled groups.
Compare the strata proportions; consider weighting when appropriate and within the student's mathematical scope.
Comparisons WITHIN each stratum may be more defensible than an unweighted population estimate.
Only applicable if sampling fractions differ and an overall population estimate is attempted.
Review
Actual stratified sampling with group proportions different from the target population, when planning an overall estimate.
Statistics
Sampling: systematic sample from an ordered list
AI13 / AA14
Could the ordering of your list line up with the selection interval?
A repeating pattern in the ordered list could produce a systematically unrepresentative sample.
Inspect the ordering and compare the selected entries under alternative starting points.
Defensible if the ordering has no relevant periodic pattern; qualify inference if it might.
Do not claim all systematic sampling is biased.
Review
Actual systematic selection from an ordered list; a plausible pattern may coincide with the interval.
Statistics
Sampling: census of a small accessible group
AI13 / AA14
Did every person in your defined group contribute usable data?
Nonresponse can produce bias even when a census was planned; a census of the club is not a census of the school.
Calculate coverage/response rate and consider who did not participate.
Results can describe the measured group when coverage and definitions support that scope.
Do not call an incomplete census a full population dataset.
Review
Student calls their collection a census of a defined group; check completeness and nonresponse.
Statistics
Small/unequal groups in sample comparison
Could one group have too few observations for a stable comparison?
Sample means/spreads or a group comparison may be sensitive to a few values; precision can differ by group.
Inspect counts, distribution, outliers and sensitivity of the comparison to individual observations.
A cautious descriptive comparison can still be useful without strong population-level inference.
No fixed universal sample-size threshold; depends on context/method.
Review
Actual group comparisons planned and available group sizes potentially unbalanced or too small for stable estimates.
Statistics
Questionnaire with self-selected responses or subjective items
Could the question wording or response scale affect the values you analyse?
Measurement validity and response bias may weaken comparisons; ordinal ratings do not have known equal intervals.
Review the exact questions and scale; inspect response patterns and consider plausible interpretations.
Explain precisely what the scores measure; avoid claims of finer accuracy or physical quantities.
Suggest only when a survey/subjective scale was actually used.
Review
Survey/questionnaire or subjective scale actually used; its response design and meanings are available to review.
Statistics
Paired measurements or comparing groups under differing conditions
Could inconsistent measurement conditions influence the observed relationship or difference?
A third variable or unmatched pairs may change correlation estimates or group comparisons.
Verify pairing by participant/observation; compare collection conditions and plausible confounders.
Interpret findings as associations within the observed conditions, not proven causal effects.
Do not imply that a correlation always has a specific confounder without evidence.
Review
Paired data or group measurements collected under potentially different conditions; consider pairing and comparability.
Statistics
Data exclusions, missing data or filtering (completion.data.processingSources)
AI13–AI16 / AA14–AA16
Could excluding missing or unusual values change the pattern you report?
Means, fitted lines, PMCC and group comparisons may be sensitive to exclusions; missingness may not be random.
Repeat a relevant calculation with/without defensible exclusions, where ethical and mathematically meaningful.
Explain and justify exclusion criteria; report sensitivity and any restricted conclusions.
Do not keep clearly erroneous readings uncritically, nor delete inconvenient real ones.
Review
Missing, excluded or filtered observations in data preparation; discuss how selection could affect later analysis.
Statistics
Secondary dataset with changes of definition or period
AI13 / AA14; plan.dataMode=secondary
Were variables measured the same way across your data sources or time periods?
Differences in definitions, units or coverage can create artificial changes/correlations.
Compare metadata, dates, units and how each variable was defined and aggregated.
Analyse only the comparable subset or qualify non-comparable periods.
Only show when data combine sources, years or measures that might be inconsistent.
Review
Secondary sources or periods combined; check whether definitions, units and coverage are genuinely comparable.
Statistics
Aggregated secondary data or subgroup averages
AI14 / AI15 / AA15 / AA16
Does a pattern between group averages necessarily describe individuals?
Associations across schools/regions can differ from individual-level associations (ecological inference issue).
Compare aggregate patterns with within-group data if available, or explicitly note unavailable individual data.
Conclude about the geographical/group-level units, not individuals.
Only show when the analysed observations are aggregate groups.
Review
Currently calculating or interpreting a relationship between aggregated group observations; NOT merely collecting aggregated data.
Statistics
Chosen PMCC / predicted linear relationship
Could curvature or one influential point make PMCC misleading here?
Pearson's r describes LINEAR association and can be strongly affected by unusual pairs.
Inspect the actual scatter plot; identify influential observations and consider whether a linear model fits.
Use PMCC for a plausible linear relationship, with any outliers addressed transparently.
Selection of PMCC alone does not prove an outlier/nonlinearity exists.
Review
Student is ACTUALLY calculating/interpreting PMCC or evaluating its linear assumption; selecting PMCC in Planning is insufficient.
Statistics / modelling
Chosen linear regression or linear-model prediction
Does your fitted line behave sensibly outside the observed values?
Extrapolated estimates may be unreliable even when the fit inside the measured range appears strong.
Inspect residual patterns and stated input domain; compare plausible alternatives at boundaries.
Restrict predictions to the observed/relevant interval or explain why wider use is defensible.
Show only for a fitted line or actual planned extrapolation; not for all graphs.
Review
Currently fitting/using a linear regression or making a line-based prediction; examine active model domain/extrapolation.
Statistics
Correlation or regression used to recommend an action
Could an unmeasured factor influence both quantities you correlated?
A statistical association does not establish that changing one variable causes the other to change.
Identify credible confounders; check subgroup patterns or discuss observational study limits.
Advice may concern association or further investigation, not a proven causal intervention.
Avoid claiming a particular confounder definitely operates without evidence.
Review
Currently interpreting correlation/regression to support advice or a potentially causal recommendation.
Statistics
Spearman rank correlation chosen
Could the relationship change direction, or do many observations share the same rank?
Rank correlation describes monotonic association; ties and non-monotonic relationships affect interpretation.
Inspect scatter plot, ranks and ties; check whether association is monotonic.
Interpret rank-based monotonic association, not necessarily a straight-line effect or causal rule.
AI SL option; do not recommend as in-course AA SL technique unless specifically added as Other.
Review
Currently computing/interpreting Spearman's rank correlation; check monotonicity/ties as applicable.
Statistics
Normal distribution model or bell-shaped prediction
Is a normal model reasonable for your observed numerical data, especially in the tails?
Skew, clusters, bounds or outliers can distort probability estimates derived from a normal model.
Inspect an appropriate histogram and summary; compare features of sample with model assumptions.
Use it as an approximation where its limits are appropriate; qualify tail probabilities.
Do not insist every dataset is normal; ensure continuous numerical context.
Review
Currently applying a normal-distribution model/probability estimate; assess fit to actual observations.
Statistics
Two-sample t-test selected
Are the observations independent and are the distribution/variance assumptions appropriate?
Misused test assumptions can make p-values or intervals misleading, especially for small or skewed samples.
Inspect study design, group distributions and unequal variability; consult course-appropriate test settings.
Use the test only where justified; otherwise frame a careful descriptive comparison or revise analysis.
Only AI SL option in current catalogue; avoid requiring a test solely to seem sophisticated.
Review
Student is performing or interpreting a two-sample t-test and relevant assumptions need evaluating.
Statistics
Chi-squared independence test selected
Are some expected cell frequencies too small for the approximation to be reliable?
A chi-squared approximation can be unreliable with very small expected counts or non-independent observations.
Calculate expected counts; inspect category definitions and sampling independence.
Combine categories only if justified or use an appropriate alternative/limited descriptive analysis.
AI SL-specific listed method; no invented universal cutoff without course guidance.
Review
Student is performing/interpreting chi-squared independence test and has expected frequencies and category counts.
Statistics
Chi-squared goodness-of-fit test selected
AI21
Do your expected category proportions and expected counts make sense?
Arbitrary expected probabilities or sparse expected frequencies undermine the reference distribution and inference.
Explain expected probabilities from a justified model; inspect expected counts and independence.
Use the test only when its expected pattern and approximation are defensible.
AI SL-specific; don't use goodness-of-fit for an unrelated association question.
Review
Student is performing/interpreting chi-squared goodness-of-fit and has a justified expected distribution.
Statistics
Binomial model / predicted repeated successes
Are the number of trials, independence and chance of success sufficiently stable?
Changes in success probability or dependence can make the binomial distribution a poor model.
Check how trials were conducted and how success was defined; inspect repeatability/variation.
Apply binomial results only over conditions where the assumptions are plausible.
Not all counts follow a binomial model; avoid assuming trials independent without reason.
Review
Student is using a binomial model to calculate probabilities or interpret outcomes, not merely collecting yes/no trials.
Statistics
Conditional probability or expected value used
AI19 / AA19
Do your probability estimates represent the actual population and conditions?
Biased probabilities or unjustified independence assumptions change conditional probabilities and expected outcomes.
Compare estimated probabilities across groups/conditions and identify assumption sources.
State the decision context and restrict expected-value advice to supported probabilities.
Require an actual probability-based method, not a vague prediction.
Review
Student is calculating conditional probability/expected value using estimates and assumptions that can be checked.
Modelling / statistics
Manual stopwatch timing chosen
AI23 / AA20 / AA25; measured time
Could reaction-time variation affect calculated speed, acceleration or rates?
Timing variation can have a larger effect on derived quantities for short intervals; excessive reported decimals are misleading.
Take repeated timings where feasible, compare variability or a better-supported timing method.
Sufficient for an approximate trend only when uncertainty does not change the conclusion.
Do not equate stopwatch display resolution with true accuracy.
Review
Timing measurements actually collected by manual stopwatch; discuss measurement variability/resolution at source.
Modelling / statistics
Video frame timing chosen
AI23 / AA20 / AA25
Could frame rate, frame selection or camera positioning limit timing accuracy?
Quantisation of video time steps and perspective can affect parameter estimates.
Identify frame interval and physical scaling; check sensitivity to one-frame shifts.
Defensible at a time scale much larger than frame uncertainty, with appropriate precision.
Only suggest if video-based measurements were selected.
Review
Timing/distance from video frames actually collected; discuss frame and calibration limits at source.
Modelling
Measured lengths/areas/volumes and geometric modelling
AI11 / AA11 / AA22
Could a small uncertainty in a length affect an area or volume estimate noticeably?
Squaring/cubing dimensions can amplify percentage uncertainty in derived areas or volumes.
Recalculate using plausible upper/lower measurement values or a simple sensitivity check.
Report a precision/range that reflects input measurements and relevant geometry.
Never assume a specific instrument tolerance without verifying it.
Review
Student is now using measured lengths in area/volume or other nonlinear geometry calculations; consider how input uncertainty changes the RESULT.
Modelling
Exponential model or percentage-growth prediction
Is a constant percentage change realistic over your entire chosen period?
Exponential models can diverge from real data when growth saturates, conditions change or rate is not constant.
Inspect residuals/observations over time and compare with a sensible alternative model.
Use only over a justified time interval; avoid long-term claims unsupported by data.
No assertion of an upper bound unless context supports one.
Review
Student is actively constructing/using an exponential model; check its assumptions and useful period.
Modelling
Polynomial/quadratic/cubic fit chosen
Could the polynomial fit measured points but behave unrealistically between or beyond them?
High-order curves can fit noise, produce artificial turning points and give unstable extrapolation.
Compare a simpler model, inspect residuals and graph outside the sample range only to test plausibility.
Restrict to a sensible domain; avoid treating a fitted turning point as physically meaningful automatically.
A true quadratic derived from geometry need not have data overfit; check fitted-vs-theoretical context.
Review
Student is actively fitting/interpreting a polynomial data model; distinguish from a theoretically derived polynomial.
Modelling
Sinusoidal/periodic prediction or model
Have you observed enough cycles to estimate the period and amplitude convincingly?
A short sequence may fit an apparent cycle that is actually a trend or irregular fluctuation.
Inspect several cycles where possible; compare phase/period stability and model residuals.
Interpret repeating behaviour only over supported conditions and duration.
Don't claim every oscillating graph is periodic.
Review
Student is actively fitting/interpreting a periodic or sinusoidal model; cycles and period estimation can be evaluated.
Modelling
Optimisation / derivative stationary point chosen
Does your optimum obey the real constraints, including endpoints and allowed dimensions?
A stationary point might be infeasible or give a local, not global, optimum; discrete design choices also matter.
Identify domain/constraints; check boundaries, feasibility and alternatives around the optimum.
Recommend an optimum only for the stated model and realistic constraints.
Don't equate differentiating to zero with proof of a global optimum.
Review
Student is finding/checking an optimum with differentiation or a model; include constraints/endpoints and interpretation.
Modelling
Power models or transformed regression
Could the model depend strongly on the range of observed positive values?
A power model fitted over a narrow range may extrapolate poorly; log transformations exclude zero/nonpositive values.
Check domain, units, plot fit/residuals and sensitivity to high/low observations.
Report model only for justified positive inputs and observed-scale conditions.
Only show for a power relationship/transform actually being used.
Review
Student is using a power law or transformed fit; positive-domain and fitted-range constraints are relevant.
Modelling
Voronoi diagram chosen
AI12
Does straight-line distance represent the 'closest' option people would actually use?
Euclidean proximity may disagree with road travel time, barriers or accessibility.
Compare a few locations using a realistic travel measure where available.
Interpret Voronoi cells as nearest in the CHOSEN metric, not automatically best service.
AI SL-specific current menu; do not assume real-world accessibility is Euclidean.
Review
Student is constructing/interpreting a Voronoi model for locations; check the distance metric and practical meaning.
Modelling
Rates of change inferred from empirical data
AI23 / AA20 / AA25
Could small variations in measured values become much larger when estimating their rate of change?
Finite differences or derivatives estimated from noisy data can be unstable.
Try reasonable intervals or smooth-model comparisons, noting how each changes the estimate.
Use rate claims only at time/space resolution supported by evidence.
If differentiation is purely analytic, measurement noise may not apply.
Review
Student is calculating/inferencing rates of change from empirically measured noisy data, not doing purely symbolic differentiation.
Modelling
Trapezoidal rule or numerical integration chosen
AI26; numeric samples
Could the spacing between data points miss important curvature?
Numerical area estimates may depend on step size when the function changes rapidly.
Compare estimates with finer spacing where available or a sensible alternative approximation.
State that the numerical estimate applies at the available sampling resolution.
AI SL catalogue option; don't assert definite error bounds without justified conditions.
Review
Student is actively applying trapezoidal rule/numerical integration to sampled values; review spacing and curvature.
Modelling
Calibrated/fitted parameters and model predictions
Did you assess the model only with the same observations used to fit it?
Good in-sample fit does not automatically demonstrate predictive accuracy on new cases.
Where feasible, compare against separate observations or describe the lack of independent validation.
Use careful within-sample conclusions if independent testing is unavailable.
Not every theoretical model requires empirical validation; only if claiming predictive fit.
Review
Student is fitting/testing a predictive model and interpreting model fit or accuracy; compare calibration/validation evidence.
Modelling
Model assumes ideal conditions/simplifications
Which simplifying assumption most changes the result when relaxed?
Neglecting friction/air resistance or treating an object as uniform can alter predicted motion/optimisation.
Compare two plausible parameter values or a more realistic case; discuss magnitude and applicability.
Retain simplification only if it doesn't change the intended practical decision materially.
Do not introduce assumptions (e.g. friction) irrelevant to the chosen model.
Review
Student is using a model with an identifiable simplifying assumption whose effect can be checked.
Theoretical / other
Mathematical claim inferred only from several numerical examples
Have you established a general claim, or only checked some examples?
A pattern observed for several inputs may fail for an untested case; examples alone do not prove all cases.
Seek a valid proof or identify conditions/possible counterexamples.
Phrase a conjecture as a conjecture until justified; restrict claims to tested cases if necessary.
Do not frame every theoretical exploration as requiring proof of a universal statement.
Review
Student is now arguing a general mathematical claim from numerical examples; proof/scope is at issue.
Theoretical / other
Algebraic derivation uses restricted domains or special cases
Could the result fail at an excluded value or outside the stated domain?
Division by an expression, inverse operations or square roots may require excluded cases or introduce extraneous solutions.
Check zero denominators, domain restrictions and converse implications; test boundary cases.
State precisely the set of inputs/conditions for which the result holds.
Use only when such algebraic restrictions actually arise.
Review
Student is doing algebra/proof involving inverses, division, roots or domain restrictions; exclusions matter now.
Modelling / statistics
Time-series observations or repeated measures from same subjects
Could observations that are close together in time or from one person be dependent?
Independence assumptions for tests or error analysis may not hold; apparent sample size can overstate information.
Inspect grouping/time ordering; compare per-person trends or residual patterns when relevant.
Conclude about the observed series/conditions and avoid unjustified independent-sample tests.
Don't impose an advanced independence test; focus on appropriate interpretation.
Review
Student is now using repeated/time-series observations in a test, regression or model where dependence assumptions matter.
Any empirical
Rounded/capped/incomplete source measurements
AI13 / AA14; data resolution
Could the recorded precision, upper limit or detection threshold hide meaningful variation?
Rounded or censored input values limit distinguishable differences and numerical precision of derived results.
Check source definitions/precision and examine whether plausible variation changes calculations or rankings.
Report results only to defensible precision and avoid conclusions about changes smaller than measurement resolution.
Only applicable where source values truly have coarse rounding or thresholds.
Review
Collected/source values are rounded, capped, censored or resolution-limited, which needs documenting before later mathematics.
